UNC7005 went further, tricking targets into linking their WhatsApp accounts to attacker devices and capturing audio and video through fake calls. Targets span government, military, defense, aerospace, academia, and think tanks across Europe and the U.S.
threatActors.beginnerTip: OAuth is the 'Sign in with Google/Microsoft' system that lets one app access your account without seeing your password, by issuing a token instead. Because the attacker uses the real login screen and steals the token, MFA does not stop it -- so scrutinize any prompt asking you to authorize a new app or link a new device.

threatActors.headline: Iran-linked hackers hit U.S. water utilities across 12 states via exposed PLCs
threatActors.body: Federal and state authorities are investigating a coordinated wave of attacks on U.S. drinking-water and wastewater facilities, with utilities in at least 12 states -- including Minnesota, Michigan, Georgia, South Dakota, and New Jersey -- affected. The activity targets internet-exposed Programmable Logic Controllers (PLC), the small industrial computers that monitor and control physical processes. The government has not formally attributed the campaign, but multiple reports and former officials point to Iran-nexus groups, echoing the 2023 CyberAv3ngers attacks on Unitronics PLCs. The spree is fueling calls for minimum cybersecurity standards, more funding, and better intelligence sharing for the water sector.
threatActors.beginnerTip: ICS/OT (Industrial Control Systems / Operational Technology) is the computer gear that runs physical equipment like pumps and valves, and a PLC is a common controller in that world. Many were built for isolated networks and have weak or default logins, so the top fix is simply getting them off the public internet and behind a VPN.

regulatory.headline: Defense contractors say CMMC confidence is rising -- but their ability to prove compliance is slipping
regulatory.body: Two new industry surveys, from Kiteworks and CyberSheath, paint a consistent picture of the U.S. Defense Industrial Base as the Cybersecurity Maturity Model Certification (CMMC) program ramps up: contractors feel more confident about their security posture, yet fewer can actually demonstrate the required controls with evidence. That gap matters because CMMC ties eligibility for Defense Department contracts to independently assessed compliance with controls drawn from NIST SP 800-171. As assessment deadlines approach, self-reported confidence without documented proof is a growing risk for suppliers.
regulatory.beginnerTip: CMMC (Cybersecurity Maturity Model Certification) is the Pentagon's program requiring contractors to meet -- and, at higher levels, prove via outside auditors -- a set baseline of cybersecurity controls before winning defense work. 'Feeling secure' is not the same as having the audit evidence; regulators care about the paperwork trail, not the vibe.

regulatory.headline: Retail-theft bill advances in Congress, raising 'very large and very dangerous' surveillance fears
regulatory.body: The Combating Organized Retail Crime Act (CORCA) cleared a significant House vote and could move quickly in the Senate. Supporters argue it would help law enforcement fight organized retail crime -- and, they say, some associated cybercrime -- by improving coordination and data sharing. Civil-liberties critics counter that the bill's information-sharing provisions could enable broad surveillance, including potential access for immigration enforcement, calling the privacy risk 'very large and very dangerous.' The debate highlights the recurring tension between anti-crime data sharing and individual privacy.
regulatory.beginnerTip: A lot of cybersecurity policy is really about who gets to collect and share data. When a crime-fighting bill expands data sharing, the security question is not just 'does it stop crime?' but 'who else can now see this data, and how is it protected?'

regulatory.headline: Fitch: water and healthcare providers can protect credit ratings by prioritizing cyber resilience
regulatory.body: In a pair of new reports, credit-rating agency Fitch said water and healthcare organizations can maintain strong credit ratings despite cyberattacks if they emphasize resilience over pure prevention. The analysts argue that because breaches are increasingly a matter of when, not if, an organization's ability to keep operating and recover quickly -- through incident response planning, backups, and continuity measures -- weighs more heavily on financial stability than trying to block every attack. It is a notable signal that cyber preparedness now factors directly into how lenders and investors judge an organization's financial health.
regulatory.beginnerTip: Resilience means designing to keep running and bounce back after an attack, not just trying to prevent one. Rating agencies deciding that recovery capability affects creditworthiness shows cybersecurity has become a mainstream financial-risk issue, not just an IT concern.

trends.headline: Policymakers push to designate AI as the next U.S. critical infrastructure sector
trends.body: A growing push in Washington would formally designate artificial intelligence as a U.S. critical infrastructure sector, a status currently held by 16 sectors such as energy, water, and finance. Backers say the label would unlock federal services, threat intelligence, and coordination resources for an industry now seen as tied to national and economic security. The move reflects how central AI systems have become -- and how their compromise could ripple across the economy -- but it also raises questions about which agency would lead and what obligations would follow.
trends.beginnerTip: 'Critical infrastructure' is the government's list of sectors so essential that their disruption would harm national security or public safety, which brings extra federal protection and scrutiny. Debating whether AI belongs on that list is really a debate about how much AI now underpins everything else.

trends.headline: New CUSTODY framework aims to constrain AI agents operating inside enterprise networks
trends.body: Security expert Jake Williams released CUSTODY, a framework for constraining Agentic AI -- AI that can take actions and make decisions on its own -- as it operates inside corporate networks. Williams said he was spurred by recent attacks involving AI systems (including incidents touching OpenAI and Hugging Face) that show autonomous agents can be abused or hijacked to move through an environment. The framework tries to put guardrails around what an AI agent is allowed to touch, reflecting a broader industry scramble to secure agents before they are widely deployed with real network access.
trends.beginnerTip: Agentic AI is AI that does not just answer questions but takes actions -- clicking, calling APIs, running commands -- to achieve a goal. That autonomy is exactly what makes it risky inside a network, so frameworks like CUSTODY focus on limiting an agent's permissions the same way you would limit a new employee's.

trends.headline: Money and mindset remain the two biggest roadblocks to effective cyber policing
trends.body: Law enforcement training is not keeping pace with the volume and rapid evolution of cybercrime, according to a Dark Reading report on the state of cyber policing. Experts argue that most officers do not need deep technical expertise -- just solid fundamentals to recognize and route digital evidence -- but limited budgets and an outdated mindset about what 'real' police work looks like keep those basics from being prioritized. The gap leaves many everyday cybercrimes under-investigated even as they grow more common.
trends.beginnerTip: A big reason cybercriminals operate with low risk is that local police often lack the training and funding to investigate digital crime. Strengthening cybersecurity is not only about better technology -- it also depends on the human and institutional capacity to actually catch offenders.

leadStory.headline: Over 9,300 exposed AWS access keys found still active years after leaking, giving full account control
leadStory.body: More than 9,300 Amazon Web Services (AWS) access keys that were publicly exposed between August 2022 and August 2026 remain active and valid, according to BleepingComputer. A valid AWS access key typically grants whoever holds it broad control over the associated cloud account, including its data, infrastructure, and billing, making a still-live leaked key a serious account-takeover risk. The report does not specify exactly where the keys were exposed, but the four-year span shows how long unrotated cloud credentials can remain a live threat once they leak. The scale points to a widespread, ongoing failure across many organizations to detect and rotate exposed secrets.
leadStory.beginnerTip: An Access Key is like a username and password combined into one string that lets software (not a person) log into a cloud account -- if it leaks in code, a config file, or a public repository, anyone who finds it can use it exactly like the real owner. Use secret-scanning tools on your repositories and rotate any key immediately if it is ever exposed.

cves.headline: Researchers show Microsoft Defender's own signed driver can be abused to kill security software at boot
cves.body: Check Point Research disclosed a technique that abuses BTR.sys, a legitimately signed Boot Time Removal Tool driver built into Microsoft Defender, to perform arbitrary kernel-level file and registry operations before Windows security software loads. The technique requires no software vulnerability and no driver imported from outside the machine, working across Windows 7 through Windows 11 25H2, because the driver itself is already trusted and signed by Microsoft. Because BTR.sys is a legitimate, signed component rather than a bug, there is no simple patch; defenders instead need to monitor and restrict how the driver's remediation functions can be invoked.
cves.beginnerTip: Windows normally only lets trusted, digitally signed drivers run at the kernel's most privileged level. This technique is in the spirit of BYOVD (Bring Your Own Vulnerable Driver) attacks, though here it abuses a built-in Defender driver rather than an imported one -- a reminder that software already trusted on your machine can sometimes be turned against it.

cves.headline: New iAuthFlow V2 phishing toolkit abuses passkeys to survive password resets
cves.body: Researchers describe a phishing toolkit called iAuthFlow V2 that can register an attacker-controlled passkey on a victim's account during a phishing session. Because the rogue passkey is a valid, registered authentication method, it lets the attacker keep signing in even after the victim changes their password and revokes active sessions. The technique turns passkeys -- normally a stronger, phishing-resistant alternative to passwords -- into a persistence mechanism when an attacker can trick a victim into authorizing one during an active phishing attack.
cves.beginnerTip: A Passkey is a newer sign-in method meant to replace passwords, tied to your device instead of something you type. This shows why account recovery matters: resetting your password is not enough if an attacker has also registered their own passkey on your account -- always review and remove authentication methods you don't recognize.

cves.headline: 14 trojanized npm packages caught dropping AI-assisted RedC2 4.0 Linux backdoor
cves.body: Trend Micro found 14 trojanized npm packages, disguised as ordinary calendar and streak-tracking utilities, that quietly drop RedC2 4.0, a Linux backdoor with an AI-assisted command-and-control component. When one of the malicious packages loads, it locates a bundled binary, marks it executable, and launches it as a detached background process, giving the attacker persistent remote access to any machine that installed it. The campaign is another example of a Supply Chain Attack that hides malicious functionality inside a package that looks legitimate on the surface, targeting developers who pull it in as a dependency.
cves.beginnerTip: A Supply Chain Attack targets trusted software you rely on -- like an open-source package -- instead of attacking you directly, so the malicious code arrives disguised as something helpful. Before adding a new dependency, check its download count, maintainer history, and recent version changes for anything unusual.

threatActors.headline: Private equity firm Apollo discloses breach tied to ongoing wave of financial-sector attacks
threatActors.body: Private equity firm Apollo disclosed that attackers broke into some of its cloud platforms during a five-day period in early July, compromising sensitive personal data. CyberScoop describes the incident as part of an ongoing wave of attacks hitting the financial sector, though the report does not name the specific data types exposed or the number of people affected. The disclosure adds Apollo to a growing list of financial firms hit by a similar pattern of intrusion this year.
threatActors.beginnerTip: When a company discloses a breach 'during a five-day period,' that window usually reflects how long attackers had access before being detected -- the shorter that gap, the less damage is typically done. If you have any relationship with an affected firm, watch for their official breach notification rather than relying on secondhand reports.

threatActors.headline: New SynkLoader malware spreads via Microsoft Teams phishing campaign
threatActors.body: A previously unknown malware family called SynkLoader is being distributed through phishing campaigns conducted over Microsoft Teams. The malware uses a fake lock screen to trick victims into typing their credentials, which it then steals. The campaign highlights how attackers continue to move phishing lures into collaboration platforms that many employees implicitly trust more than email.
threatActors.beginnerTip: A fake lock screen mimics your computer's normal login prompt to trick you into typing your password into a malicious program instead of the real operating system. If a Teams message ever prompts you to "unlock" or re-enter credentials unexpectedly, verify through another channel before typing anything.

threatActors.headline: Banking trojans Manic, Grandoreiro, and ToxicPanda 2.0 remain active threats
threatActors.body: SecurityWeek highlights three active banking-trojan operations: Manic, which comes equipped with spyware capabilities; a persistent Grandoreiro campaign continuing to target Latin America and Europe; and an expanded ToxicPanda 2.0 malware family. Grandoreiro in particular has resurfaced repeatedly despite past law-enforcement takedowns, refining its evasion and detection-avoidance features. Together, the campaigns show banking trojans remain a durable, evolving threat to financial-account holders across multiple regions.
threatActors.beginnerTip: A Banking Trojan is malware disguised as something legitimate that specifically targets your online banking credentials and transactions once installed. These families keep resurfacing because takedowns remove infrastructure, not the developers -- treat unexpected banking-app prompts or login pages with suspicion.

regulatory.headline: Lawmakers seek GAO watchdog review of federal government's hacking tools used on Americans
regulatory.body: Sen. Ron Wyden and Rep. Greg Casar are asking the Government Accountability Office (GAO) to investigate how federal agencies use spyware and other sophisticated hacking tools and authorities domestically. The request reflects growing congressional concern over the scope of government hacking capabilities directed at Americans and calls for an independent watchdog review rather than relying solely on agency self-reporting.
regulatory.beginnerTip: The GAO is a nonpartisan federal watchdog that investigates how agencies spend money and use their authority, then reports findings to Congress. Requests like this one are how lawmakers try to get independent facts about surveillance programs that are otherwise largely secret.

regulatory.headline: Defense contractors' CMMC confidence keeps rising even as their ability to prove compliance lags
regulatory.body: A new consulting-firm survey finds a widening confidence gap among U.S. defense contractors preparing for Cybersecurity Maturity Model Certification (CMMC): self-reported confidence in their security posture keeps climbing even as fewer contractors say they can actually document and prove the required controls. The disconnect matters because CMMC ties eligibility for Defense Department contracts to independently assessed, evidence-backed compliance rather than self-assessment alone.
regulatory.beginnerTip: CMMC is the Pentagon's certification program requiring defense contractors to prove -- with audit evidence, not just self-assessment -- that they meet baseline cybersecurity controls. Feeling secure and being able to demonstrate it to an auditor are two different things, and only the second one satisfies a compliance requirement.

trends.headline: OWASP releases new Top 10 blueprint flagging AI agent skill risks
trends.body: The Open Worldwide Application Security Project (OWASP) published a new top-10 security list tailored to AI-era risks, introducing a Universal Skill Format meant to bring consistency and security review to the growing ecosystem of AI "skills" and add-ons that extend chatbot and agent capabilities. The framework reflects OWASP's ongoing effort to give developers and security teams a standard way to evaluate risk in fast-moving AI tooling, much as its original Top 10 did for web applications.
trends.beginnerTip: OWASP is a nonprofit best known for its Top 10 lists of the most critical security risks in a given technology area, widely used by developers as a baseline checklist. A new list for AI "skills" signals that add-on capabilities for AI agents are now common enough to need their own standardized security guidance.

trends.headline: OpenAI adds new AI security controls following the Hugging Face incident
trends.body: OpenAI rolled out new security controls for its AI systems, a move Dark Reading frames as a follow-up to last month's incident involving Hugging Face. The report suggests some of the added protections arguably should have existed before autonomous, Agentic AI models were deployed with real-world reach. The update is part of a broader industry pattern of retrofitting guardrails onto AI agents only after an incident exposes a gap.
trends.beginnerTip: When AI vendors add security controls reactively -- after an incident rather than before deployment -- it's a sign the industry is still catching up to the risks of giving AI systems real autonomy. If you deploy AI agents in your own environment, don't assume vendor-side guardrails alone are sufficient; add your own permission boundaries too.

trends.headline: Volunteer push grows to help under-resourced local governments defend against cyberattacks
trends.body: Dark Reading reports on efforts to recruit volunteer cybersecurity professionals to help defend municipal and other local government agencies that operate with far smaller security budgets than federal counterparts or private industry. Small government IT teams are common targets for ransomware and other attacks but often lack the staff or funding to build a dedicated security program. Community and volunteer initiatives are positioned as one way to help close that gap in the near term.
trends.beginnerTip: Local governments -- cities, counties, school districts -- are frequent ransomware targets because they often run critical services on thin IT budgets with little dedicated security staff. Efforts to bring in volunteer expertise reflect a real, ongoing resource gap at the local level, not just at federal agencies.

A new malware family is spreading through built-in updaters on Android-based vehicle head units to enable ad fraud and build a proxy botnet, Kaspersky reports.
Former NSA Director Paul Nakasone has launched the Nakasone Group, a new advisory firm counseling government and corporate clients on cybersecurity and national-security risk.
SecurityWeek's weekly roundup covers a 'zombie card' payment attack, T-Mobile reportedly cutting a cable to stop hackers, and GitHub denying that AI caused a recent bug.
